stances.claim: The disjunctive word 'or' must be read as providing an alternative option as a general rule — and on the People v. XXX facts, 'first cousin' (a relative of the fourth degree) and 'relative within the third civil degree of consanguinity' are different relationships, so the 'or' impermissibly let prosecutors elevate the charge to qualified rape and double-track the proof.
stances.rhetorical_move: statutory-construction lesson applied to a real charging defect
stances.evidence: General rule on disjunctive 'or'; Civil Code degree-of-consanguinity rules; the actual wording of the information

stances.claim: Counsel's pre-trial stipulation that the accused was a relative within the third civil degree was a 'palpable mistake, bordering on recklessness and utter incompetence' because the determination of relationship by civil degree is basic Civil Code application that every lawyer ought to know — and parties cannot stipulate to an erroneous application of law even where Section 1 Rule 118 allows fact-stipulation.
stances.evidence: Civil Code; CPRA; SC's own characterization of the stipulation

stances.claim: The Court properly downgraded the conviction from qualified rape to simple rape, preserving the conviction on the carnal-knowledge core while declining to give the prosecution alternative-track elevation it did not properly plead and prove.
stances.evidence: Simple-rape elements satisfied; qualifying circumstances not adequately pleaded

stances.claim: All three court-actors share a prime duty 'to see that justice is done': (1) prosecutors under the newly promulgated CPRA; (2) defense counsel via fiduciary duty of competence and diligence; (3) the bench through duty to intervene when stipulations contravene law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy.

notable_anecdotes: The information's literal use of 'first cousin OR relative within the third civil degree of consanguinity' — with the author rendering the disjunctive in all caps (OR) to spotlight the prosecutorial drafting error.
The CPRA framing of the prosecutorial duty — 'not to convict, but to see that justice is done' — used as the column's normative anchor for the three-actor reminder.
The Court's blunt rebuke of defense counsel: 'palpable mistake, bordering on recklessness and utter incompetence' — a rare uncovered judicial characterization of counsel performance.
The structural irony surfaced: a defective information (prosecutor's error) plus a defective stipulation (defense counsel's error) carried 'mindlessly' through RTC and CA — only corrected at the SC.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes People v. XXX (Supreme Court, promulgated July 25, 2023, released recently), in which the Court -- reviewing a Court of Appeals (Cagayan de Oro) decision affirming the Regional Trial Court (Cagayan de Oro) -- upheld the conviction for simple rape only, not qualified rape, because of the prosecutors' use of the word 'or' in the information. The accused was named 'XXX' to comply with anonymization laws. Simple rape (under settled jurisprudence) is committed by carnal knowledge through force or intimidation, or when the victim is deprived of reason or unconscious, or under 12 years of age. Under RPC Article 266-B-1, simple rape becomes qualified -- a more serious offense -- when committed by a relative by consanguinity or affinity within the third civil degree of a victim below 18, and both qualifying circumstances of minority and relationship must be alleged in the information. The information here alleged that the 'accused, knowing fully well the minority of his first cousin OR relative within the third civil degree of consanguinity through force and intimidation and through grave abuse of authority... feloniously insert[ed] his penis into the vagina of' the victim. The victim's minority (15 years old) was proven by certified birth certificate; the relationship rested on a pre-trial stipulation that the accused was 'a relative within the third civil degree of consanguinity.'
